problem: Our reporting page loads one frozen daily snapshot of about two million integers and then answers roughly fifty thousand 'combined total between position i and position j' requests against it. Nothing in the snapshot ever changes between loads. What should we precompute at load time?

A leaderboard holds one number per player. Individual players' numbers are revised a few thousand times a second, one at a time, and we simultaneously have to answer 'what do players ranked a through b add up to' constantly. Only ever one cell changes at a time, never a stretch.

An operator can add a fixed amount to every slot in a chosen window of our scheduling grid, and can separately ask for the combined value of some other arbitrary window. Both the writes and the reads cover whole stretches, never single cells.

A terrain heightmap is loaded once at startup and is never written to again. The renderer asks for the largest value inside an arbitrary span millions of times inside a frame budget. Preparation cost at startup is irrelevant; the per-question cost has to be constant.

The quantity we need over a window is 'how many distinct values it contains', which does not combine cleanly from the answers for two halves. We can, however, cheaply keep a summary for each fixed chunk of the array, and we would rather write something simple than a heavy deferred-update tree.

A road network with about four hundred thousand junctions and nine hundred thousand one-way links. Every traversal time is a positive number of seconds. We need the quickest route from one depot to every junction.
In our maze, stepping onto an open tile costs nothing at all and breaking through a wall costs exactly one unit. There is no third cost. Find the cheapest way from the entrance to the exit.

A currency arbitrage checker: some conversions increase value, so a few of the transition costs come out below zero. We need distances from one starting currency, and we also want to know whether a loop exists that keeps gaining.
A factory has one hundred and eighty stations. At boot we want to fill in a table giving the distance between every ordered pair of them, once, and then never recompute it.
We scan one large log file for a single fixed signature and need every offset at which it appears, in time linear in the file, without adding a dependency.
A moderation filter holds forty thousand forbidden phrases, and every incoming document has to be checked against all of them in a single pass over the document.

A similarity tool repeatedly asks whether the stretch of document A from i to j is character-for-character the same as the stretch of document B from p to q, for millions of index pairs chosen at run time.
The statement caps the number of items at nine, and the answer depends on the sequence in which they are processed, so every arrangement is a different candidate. One second of runtime.
There are up to eighteen jobs and each one is either taken or left, with the value of a selection depending on exactly which combination was chosen. One second of runtime.
The count goes up to thirty-six and each element is either included or not, so the obvious enumeration is far beyond the limit, while the values themselves are far too large to index any table by.
The array length is capped at four thousand and we have one second. Can we afford to consider every pair of positions, and where exactly is the ceiling on that?
The array can hold one hundred thousand entries with a one second limit. Is looking at every pair of positions still affordable here, and if not, what is the budget?
The whole input is a single integer that can reach a quintillion, and we must output a count derived from it. Walking over anything is obviously out of the question.
A deduplication pass asks 'have I encountered this thirty-two byte fingerprint before' about a billion times. Nothing ever has to come back out in any particular sequence.
A booking system must answer 'what is the latest reservation starting before two in the afternoon' and must also walk every reservation chronologically. Reservations are added and cancelled all day.
A live scoreboard must report how many players currently stand above a given player, and separately who currently occupies position five hundred, while players join and drop out continuously.
Our keys are opcode numbers from zero to two hundred and fifty-five and nearly all of them are in use. We want the cheapest possible lookup with a hard guarantee rather than an expected one.
A one-shot command-line tool parses a file, builds a tree of nodes, prints a report and exits. Releasing individual nodes would be pure bookkeeping for a process that is about to end anyway.
An embedded routine can prove when compiling that it will never need more than four kilobytes, and the target has no heap we are willing to touch at all.

We are publishing a parsing package. We have no idea whether the program using it runs on bare metal, inside a test harness, or in a long-lived server, and we do not want to make that choice for them.

I wrote an object of route definitions directly in the file and the compiler widened every one of its string values to the general string type. I own the literal and want it pinned exactly as written.
I control the helper function's signature and I want callers to get narrow types out of the array they type inline at the call, without asking every caller to append anything to their argument.

The function comes from a third-party package whose signature I cannot change, and it keeps widening my fixed-length argument into a plain array of strings. I need the narrow types to survive before they reach it.

My generic function takes a list of allowed values and a fallback. Passing a fallback that is not in the list quietly broadens the type parameter instead of being rejected. I want that second parameter to stop contributing candidates.
I want my configuration object validated against a shape, but the moment I declare it with that shape every entry collapses to the shape's union and I lose the specific type each entry actually had.
I want one line inside an ordinary source file to assert that the expression below it does not compile, and I want the check itself to start failing the day that expression becomes legal.
A tiny utility library with no dependencies and no test runner at all. I want to assert that a computed type is exactly the expected one using nothing but the compiler itself.
We already run Vitest. I want fluent assertions about types living in the same files as the runtime tests, with no extra command in CI and nothing to compile separately.
Our package ships declarations and we want a standalone command in CI that reads dedicated assertion files and reports failures, including cases where an expression was supposed to be rejected.

We maintain declarations in the community-run upstream repository and have to demonstrate they behave correctly across several compiler releases simultaneously, following that repository's own conventions.

About eight hundred identical crates, each needing its own placement and its own pointer handler, written as ordinary children in JSX. We want them submitted to the GPU once while keeping normal React ergonomics.
The repeated shapes arrive as existing meshes inside a loaded glTF file rather than as geometry we wrote, and we need several hundred of each without paying a separate submission per copy.
We loaded one model and want six copies of the whole thing placed around the level, sharing the original buffers rather than duplicating them in memory.
Our bottleneck is triangle count rather than submission count: one very dense rock looks right up close but wastes the GPU at distance. We already have three quality versions of it.
Rows already arrive grouped by when they were received, and we now reorder them by urgency. Two rows of equal urgency must still come out in the sequence they arrived in.
We order twenty million values, all of them whole numbers between zero and one hundred thousand. The library call that compares elements is the measured bottleneck.
We order a list of records by the lowercased form of one field, and producing that form is not free. At the moment it is being recomputed over and over while the ordering happens.
We need the median salary out of fifty million records, once. Nothing downstream cares about the arrangement of anything else.
A loop constructs a fresh growable list of known final length on every iteration, and the profiler shows the cost is repeated growth inside that loop.
A struct on our hottest path carries a list that almost always holds two or three items, yet every single instance still reaches out to the heap for it.
A compiler pass creates millions of tiny nodes that all become garbage together when the pass ends, and comparing two of them currently walks their entire structure.
The profile shows no single hot call site at all; the cost is spread thinly and evenly across thousands of small allocations throughout the whole program.
A reviewer moves through the page with the keyboard and cannot tell where they currently are. A stylesheet reset early in the project removed the browser's default marker and nothing was put back.
The dismiss control in the corner of our cards occupies eighteen by eighteen and testers on phones keep missing it. What dimension are we actually required to hit?
Our body copy is a light grey on white. Someone asked what ratio we are obliged to reach, and whether the faint sample text inside each field counts for that purpose.
Our inputs communicate their purpose only through the greyed sample text sitting inside them, and assistive technology announces nothing at all when focus arrives.
The page jumps straight from the document title to a much smaller sub-title because the designer wanted a smaller size there, and assistive technology users say the document outline is confusing.
A user reports that the scrolling depth effect on our landing page makes them feel sick, and asks whether we respect the setting they turned on in their operating system.
Text on the article page drops down half a second after load, every single time, as the illustrations arrive.
The gallery page transfers fourteen megabytes. The files are camera-resolution originals and they are displayed at postage-stamp size.
Everything is themed except that selecting text gives the stock blue, the scroll gutter is the operating system's own, and the figures in our table jitter sideways as they update.
After an hour with the dashboard open the tab holds nine hundred megabytes and interaction lags. Reloading fixes it. Each panel opens a socket and starts a repeating timer.
Our toolbar mixes a drawn arrow with a couple of characters typed straight into the markup, and the result looks different on a Mac than on Windows.
Our accordion grows from nothing to its natural size and the whole page stutters on a mid-range laptop while it opens.
Reviewers say our transitions feel sluggish. A button's press feedback and a whole view change are both set to six hundred milliseconds. What should each of those actually be?
Every card that enters overshoots its resting place and springs back. A stakeholder said the product feels like a children's toy.
Someone added a rendering hint permanently to the card class to 'make it smooth'. Memory use climbed and scrolling got measurably worse.
Our animated mark keeps running while the tab sits in the background, and laptop users complain about the fan.
Support has three identical orders from the same customer within a second of each other. The customer says nothing appeared to happen when they first pressed the control.
A user completed our twelve-field form, the server rejected one value, and the page came back with everything wiped. They did not attempt it again.
Testers start typing into a field, forget what it was asking for, and have to delete everything they wrote in order to read the prompt again.
Whether you have not created an account yet, searched for something with no matches, or lack permission to view the list, our table shows the same grey box.
The administration table draws all fourteen thousand of its rows at once. Scrolling it is unusable on anything but a desktop.
A change adds functions spelled like getUserName and a file called userStuff.ml. What does the house style say about how those should have been written?
The new file declares a type called order_t alongside six functions, inside a module that is already called Order. A reviewer says the name repeats itself.
We have parseInt in one place, intFromString in another and makeIntOfString in a third, all doing the same job. What should all three have been called?
One lookup hands back nothing when the key is missing and another throws. Both are spelled the same way in different modules and callers cannot tell them apart at the call site.
Half our functions take a trailing true or false and nobody can read the call sites without opening the definition to find out what it means.
A function takes two integers meaning a starting offset and a count. Someone reversed them at a call site, it compiled cleanly, and it shipped.
We are starting a fresh system for the web and need nine steps per hue that read as evenly spaced to the eye without hand-correcting each one. Which space should the tokens be authored in?
We produced our night theme in an afternoon by programmatically flipping the day theme's values. Everything now looks flat and sits on one plane.
Our cards sit on a deep indigo panel and the supporting line under each title uses our standard neutral five hundred. It reads as though the styling failed to load.
This dashboard has a teal header, an orange call to action, purple tags, a green sidebar and red alerts. It feels busy rather than rich.
Our brand blue is on the confirm control, the hero background, three icons and a decorative rule. Users report they cannot find the control.
We drive a geometry's subdivision count from a slider, and the object flickers and loses its GPU-side state every time the slider moves.
We want to set only the x component of a rotation, and only the far plane of a shadow's camera, without constructing an object for either one.
We render a custom class that is not part of the scene graph as a child of a mesh, and nothing happens. How does a child become a named property of its parent in this renderer?
We share one loaded texture across several components. The moment any one of them goes away, the others turn black.
Our component renders the canvas element and also asks for the renderer state in the same function body. It crashes on mount.
We keep a Python list ordered by placing each new element at its located position. We expected logarithmic behaviour and the loop is unmistakably quadratic.
Under memory pressure our C++ ordering call gets noticeably slower, but only sometimes, and the code path taken never changes.
Our recursive tree walk kills the interpreter on deep inputs. A colleague suggested simply raising the ceiling to a million.
We implemented union-find with only one of the two standard improvements and measured logarithmic behaviour per query rather than the near-constant figure the textbook quotes.
Our rolling fingerprint uses a single prime near a billion. Across a million pairwise comparisons we started seeing false matches.
